answer_text:
Switching to the metric system in the United States would be **extremely difficult** — arguably one of the most complex logistical and cultural undertakings in American history. Here's a breakdown of the key challenges and considerations:

---

## 🏛️ Historical & Political Background

U.S. customary units have been defined in terms of metric units since the 19th century, and, according to U.S. law, the SI (metric) system has been the "preferred system of weights and measures for United States trade and commerce" since 1975. Under Executive Order 12770, signed in 1991 by President George H.W. Bush, all U.S. agencies were required to adopt the metric system. However, conversion was made not mandatory, so U.S. customary units remain in common use in government and many industries.

In 1968, a study was approved by Congress which recommended a national conversion to metric units. Again, the movement was stymied by lack of popular support — a Gallup poll that year showed that 45% of Americans were opposed to the switch.

---

## 💰 The Cost

The biggest reasons the U.S. hasn't adopted the metric system are simply time and money. When the Industrial Revolution began in the country, expensive manufacturing plants became a main source of American jobs and consumer products. Because the Imperial System was in place at that time, the machinery used in factories was developed to size in Imperial units. Whenever the discussion of switching arose in Congress, the passage of a bill favoring the metric system was thwarted by big businesses and citizens who didn't want to go through the time-consuming and expensive hassle of changing the country's entire infrastructure.

We only have to look to Canada to get a sense of what switching would take. Canada went metric back in 1970, and it took about 15 years and more than $1 billion to update everything. The U.S. is roughly 10 times the size of Canada, so the costs would be vastly larger.

One expert attempted to calculate the cost to the U.S. of *maintaining the status quo*, estimating in 2008 that the cost is in the ballpark of $1.28 trillion per year. These losses stem from mistakes caused by conversion errors, buying and maintaining two sets of inventory, lost time teaching two systems, and jobs lost when international companies avoid working with U.S. companies still using U.S. customary.

---

## 🏗️ Infrastructure Overhaul

Every speed limit sign would have to be changed from miles per hour to kilometers per hour — and so would every sign on every city street, country road, and freeway across the nation. Beyond road signs, tools, machinery, blueprints, appliances, and countless other systems would all need to be replaced or recalibrated.

---

## 📚 Education

The education system is perhaps the hardest hit. Both U.S. Customary and Metric are taught, but students required to learn two measurement systems will more likely be confused, and the additional time spent teaching both systems has its own implied cost. On the flip side, metric calculations can generally be completed 45% faster, and a full conversion to the metric system is estimated to save roughly $17.6 billion in educational costs.

---

## ⚠️ Safety Risks During Transition

Accidents caused by mixing up the two systems are a real danger. They stem from using two different systems of measurement: customary (used mainly in the U.S.) and metric (used just about everywhere else). For example, a NASA probe's failure to use metric units in its software led it to be around 170 kilometers lower than planned, costing $125 million.

---

## 🌍 Scale of the Challenge

When the rest of the world switched to metric, it was mostly before or at the very beginning of the industrial revolution. Today, with mass production of goods, switching everything over to a new measurement system would be a gigantic undertaking — the largest, most complex transition of measurement systems in human history.

---

## ✅ The Silver Lining: The US Is Already Partly Metric

Coke bottles are sold in liters, so is wine. Medicine is measured in milligrams. Food nutrition labels are metric. And what about a 100-meter sprint or a 5K race? So a full transition, while massive, wouldn't be starting from zero.

---

**In summary**, switching to the metric system would be incredibly difficult — requiring enormous financial investment, an overhaul of infrastructure, a cultural shift, and years (possibly decades) of transition. The political will has repeatedly failed to materialize, and the voluntary nature of past legislation means the U.S. has been slowly, partially metrifying for decades without ever fully committing.
